title: Naseeruddin Shah Looks Exactly Like JRD Tata. Jim Sarbh Matches Him Frame for Frame. The Titan Story Is Free to Stream.
excerpt: Made In India: A Titan Story is a six-episode love letter to Indian enterprise — and the two lead performances make it unmissable for anyone who grew up with a Titan on their wrist.
body:
There is a moment early in **Made In India: A Titan Story** when **Naseeruddin Shah**, playing **JRD Tata**, leans forward in his chair and tells a young executive that the Tatas should not just help build India into a superpower — they should help build it into a happy country. It is a quiet line, delivered with the kind of measured warmth that makes you sit up straighter. And then you notice the resemblance. The bearing. The silver hair. The way authority sits lightly on his shoulders. Shah does not just play JRD Tata. He *becomes* him.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=MPNexsJZycw</youtube>

This is the engine of the show. Directed by **Robbie Grewal** and now streaming for free on **Amazon MX Player**, the six-episode series chronicles the improbable birth of **Titan** — how a stubborn Tata executive named **Xerxes Desai** convinced his company, his country, and eventually the world that India could put a world-class watch on millions of wrists. It is adapted from journalist **Vinay Kamath's** book *Titan: Inside India's Most Successful Consumer Brand*, and it plays like something between a corporate thriller and a love story about manufacturing.

**Jim Sarbh** plays Xerxes with his now-familiar cocktail of eccentricity and restless intelligence — impulsive, occasionally manipulative, driven by an ego that he is charming enough to make you forgive. The performance feels alive in every frame. When Xerxes returns to the Tata Group from a stint at NBIDC and immediately gets bored at his desk, Sarbh makes you feel the itch in his bones. When he discovers that imported watches are the most smuggled items in the country and sees an entire industry hiding in that statistic, the gleam in his eye is worth the subscription price — except there is no subscription price.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DY6YVgStxA1/

The show is set in pre-liberalisation India, a period that the production design recreates with meticulous care. Bombay, Bangalore, and Hosur across the late 1970s and 1980s are rendered with the kind of texture that no amount of digital grading alone can deliver. The cinematography by **Aditya Kapur** is clean and elegant, and the use of old Hindi film songs as temporal signposts — *Kya Hua Tera Vaada* gets a particularly well-timed deployment — adds a layer of authenticity that feels earned rather than nostalgic for nostalgia's sake.

The supporting cast does solid work. **Vaibhav Tatwawadi** plays the grounded counterpoint to Xerxes' romanticism, and **Kaveri Seth** and **Lakshvir Singh Saran** bring genuine warmth to the ensemble. But make no mistake: this show belongs to its two leads. **Filmfare** gave it 4 out of 5, calling Shah's JRD Tata "a masterclass and proof that skill is impervious to time." Multiple reviewers have called it the best Indian OTT drama of the season.

> "Just Naseeruddin Shah's JRD Tata is reason enough to watch this show. It's a performance so physically uncanny that it makes you wish the show had been built around him entirely." — Filmfare

Where the show stumbles slightly is in its episodic structure. Some conflicts — particularly the European chapter, where Titan's international credibility is on the line — resolve with less dramatic weight than they deserve. The writing establishes obstacles clearly but does not always burrow deep enough into them. It is a minor complaint in a show where two actors of this calibre are constantly rescuing every scene.

For the diaspora, this is personal viewing. If you grew up in an Indian household, there was a Titan on someone's wrist — your father's, your uncle's, maybe the one your grandmother received as a retirement gift. The brand is woven into the fabric of middle-class aspiration. To see how it was born — in the face of Swiss scepticism, government red tape, and domestic doubters who did not believe India could compete — is to understand something essential about the country's self-image.

All six episodes are streaming now on **Amazon MX Player**, completely free, no subscription required. In the US, UK, and Canada, you can watch it on the same platform. At roughly an hour per episode, it is a comfortable weekend binge — and the two performances at its centre are worth every minute.

If you have ever worn a Titan watch, or if your parents ever gifted you one, this show will make you want to call home.
